prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

LONDON, England (CNN) -- Police officers responsible for protecting the British royal family handled firearms when drunk, traded pornography and steroids and sat on Queen Elizabeth II's throne in comical poses, it has been alleged in a London court. The former royal protection officer was responsible for security at Buckingham Palace. The allegations were made Tuesday by John Cooper, the lawyer for former royal protection officer Paul Page, who is accused of defrauding colleagues and friends to fund a life of luxury, The British Press Association reported. According to PA, the claims were made during a lengthy cross-examination of Adam McGregor, a colleague of Page who left service at London's Buckingham Palace in 2005, who has accused the former officer of "conning" him out of thousands of dollars. At one point Cooper "suggested" there had been a procedure among armed officers at the palace whereby one officer on duty would sleep while the others kept watch for their superior. McGregor denied any knowledge of this and all other allegations of wrongdoing among his colleagues at the iconic Royal residence. However, when pressed further he did admit to sitting on one of the thrones, but did not recall doing any "comical poses." The court also heard that officers protecting the royals lost more than £250,000 ($365,800) to a spread betting venture called "The Currency Club," one of a number of apparently successful sidelines Page allegedly set up to clear spiraling debts, PA said. According to the BBC, Page extracted around £3 million ($4.4 million) from some 57 lenders or investors. Cooper suggested that McGregor had been "one of those police officers" using mobile patrols to deliver cash to other police officers based in Royal Protection who were involved in financial matters. The accusation was again denied by McGregor. He instead claimed he had been "totally sucked in" by Page. "I was totally sucked in by Paul he is a very charismatic person," he said, before adding that he had acted "very naively and very stupidly" in some of his dealings with his former colleague. The prosecution claimed much of the money was promptly laundered by Page's wife before being gambled away, as Page himself hid his dishonesty behind a " veneer of credibility" fueled by a fleet of expensive cars and claims he was a highly "adept" property developer and market speculator, PA said. Father of five Page, 37, from Essex in south-east England, has denied five charges -- two of fraudulent trading, one of intimidation, threatening to take revenge and making a threat to kill between January 1, 2003 and March 30, 2007. His wife Laura, 42, denied "being concerned in an arrangement facilitating dealings with criminal property," intimidation and threatening to kill.

outputs.L1:
LONDON, England (CNN) — Police officers assigned to protect the British royal family allegedly handled firearms while drunk, traded pornography and steroids, and sat on Queen Elizabeth II’s throne in comical poses, a London court has heard.

The allegations, reported by the British Press Association, were made Tuesday by John Cooper, the lawyer for former royal protection officer Paul Page, who was responsible for security at Buckingham Palace. Page is accused of defrauding colleagues and friends to fund a life of luxury.

According to PA, the claims emerged during a lengthy cross-examination of Adam McGregor, a former colleague of Page who left service at London’s Buckingham Palace in 2005. McGregor has accused Page of “conning” him out of thousands of dollars.

At one point, Cooper suggested that armed officers at the palace had operated under an arrangement in which one officer on duty would sleep while the others kept watch for their superior. McGregor denied any knowledge of that claim and of all other allegations of wrongdoing among his colleagues at the iconic royal residence.

However, when pressed further, McGregor admitted that he had sat on one of the thrones, though he said he did not recall striking any “comical poses.”

The court also heard that officers protecting the royals lost more than £250,000 ($365,800) in a spread-betting venture called “The Currency Club,” one of several apparently successful sidelines that Page allegedly established to address spiraling debts, PA said.

According to the BBC, Page obtained around £3 million ($4.4 million) from some 57 lenders or investors.

Cooper suggested that McGregor had been “one of those police officers” who used mobile patrols to deliver cash to other police officers in Royal Protection who were involved in financial matters. McGregor again denied the accusation, saying instead that he had been “totally sucked in” by Page.

“I was totally sucked in by Paul; he is a very charismatic person,” McGregor said, adding that he had acted “very naively and very stupidly” in some of his dealings with his former colleague.

The prosecution claimed that much of the money was promptly laundered by Page’s wife before being gambled away, while Page himself concealed his dishonesty behind a “veneer of credibility” sustained by a fleet of expensive cars and claims that he was a highly “adept” property developer and market speculator, PA said.

Page, a 37-year-old father of five from Essex in southeast England, has denied five charges: two of fraudulent trading, one of intimidation, one of threatening to take revenge, and one of making a threat to kill between January 1, 2003, and March 30, 2007.

His wife, Laura Page, 42, has denied “being concerned in an arrangement facilitating dealings with criminal property,” intimidation, and threatening to kill.

LONDON, England (CNN) — A London court has heard allegations that police assigned to guard the British royal family handled guns while intoxicated, exchanged pornography and steroids, and posed jokingly on Queen Elizabeth II’s throne.

The claims concerned officers involved in royal protection, including a former officer who had worked in security at Buckingham Palace. They were raised Tuesday by John Cooper, attorney for ex-royal protection officer Paul Page, according to the British Press Association. Page is accused of cheating friends and fellow officers out of money to support an extravagant lifestyle.

PA reported that the accusations emerged during an extended cross-examination of Adam McGregor, a former colleague of Page who left his post at Buckingham Palace in 2005. McGregor has alleged that Page “conned” him out of thousands of dollars.

During questioning, Cooper suggested that armed officers at the palace had a practice in which one officer on duty would sleep while the others watched out for supervisors. McGregor said he knew nothing about that claim or any other misconduct by colleagues at the well-known royal residence. When questioned further, however, he acknowledged that he had sat on one of the thrones, though he said he could not remember striking any humorous poses.

The court was also told that royal protection officers lost more than £250,000, or about $365,800, in a spread-betting scheme known as “The Currency Club.” PA described it as one of several seemingly successful side ventures Page allegedly created to deal with mounting debts.

The BBC reported that Page obtained about £3 million, or $4.4 million, from roughly 57 lenders or investors.

Cooper also suggested that McGregor had been among police officers who used mobile patrols to transport cash to other Royal Protection officers involved in financial dealings. McGregor denied that allegation as well. He said instead that Page had completely drawn him in.

“I was totally sucked in by Paul; he is a very charismatic person,” McGregor said, adding that he had behaved “very naively and very stupidly” in some of his dealings with his former colleague.

Prosecutors alleged that much of the money was quickly laundered by Page’s wife and then lost through gambling. They said Page concealed his dishonesty behind a “veneer of credibility,” supported by expensive cars and by claims that he was a skilled property developer and market speculator, PA reported.

Page, a 37-year-old father of five from Essex in southeast England, has denied five charges: two counts of fraudulent trading, one count of intimidation, threatening revenge, and making a threat to kill, covering the period from January 1, 2003, to March 30, 2007.

His wife, Laura Page, 42, has denied being involved in an arrangement that facilitated dealings with criminal property, as well as intimidation and threatening to kill.
